stances.claim: After two decades of seemingly interminable disputes (local litigations + international arbitration in Singapore and Washington, DC), NAIA 3 is still mired in controversy and unfinished both physically and legally. The physical and legal aspects are intertwined -- Transportation Sec Joseph E. A. Abaya recently announced an additional P1.9 billion to complete the terminal in August 2014; on the legal front, the latest is the CA's Republic v. Piatco decision (Aug 7 2013, J. Brusellas) fixing just compensation at $371 million, modifying the RTC Pasay $176M earlier judgment.

Both courts used the Republic's $300M 'replacement cost' as of Dec 2002 'when construction ceased' -- but the RTC subtracted deterioration/depreciation and Piatco-noncompliance deductions, while the CA did not (ruling these were already factored in) and imposed 6% interest under RA 8974 because the Republic should have paid the $300M when it took over in 2004. Both courts rejected Piatco's $900M-plus-12%-interest claim.

Before deciding whether to appeal to the SC, the government should first review the arbitration proceedings -- both the Singapore and Washington panels dismissed Piatco's claims without any award; but at Fraport AG's (the German shareholder's) initiative, a second ICSID panel annulled the first; a third ICSID panel is now hearing the compensation claim all over again. To prevent possible double payment, retired Justice Florentino P. Feliciano (the Philippine counsel) should be consulted.

The overall legal strategy of the Republic should be reviewed. In 1993, AEDC's six-taipan 'unsolicited proposal' was challenged by Piatco; both offered to build NAIA 3 for at least $350M at no government cost and pay 5% (escalating to 10%) of gross revenues for 25 years; AEDC guaranteed P135M while Piatco offered P17.75 BILLION -- Piatco won. But after the 1997 concession contract, the government executed a new agreement and three supplements giving substantial benefits to Piatco -- Agan v. Piatco (May 5 2003, J. Puno) invalidated them. Instead of taking over the terminal temporarily under police power (not eminent domain) as Puno ruled, the government -- 'for reasons I cannot fathom up to now' -- instituted the long-winded expropriation case in RTC Pasay (and later CA).

The more expeditious way was to ask the SC directly (in Agan v. Piatco) to fix compensation for the takeover. As a sitting member of the Court at that time, CJP wrote a separate opinion invalidating the Piatco contracts for 'being riddled with irregularities galore and blatant violations of law and public policy, far too many to ignore' -- but to avoid unjust enrichment for the government, opined that Piatco, its subcontractors, investors, and lenders should be reimbursed actual and reasonable construction expenses. CJP also suggested the government bid out the operation under BOT-analogous principles -- with payment to builder/funders/investors/contractors staggered and scheduled into the bids alongside annual guaranteed government payments. The terminal could be completed and operated immediately without any expense but with sure income -- however, both the SC's ruling on temporary takeover and CJP's practical suggestion were ignored.

NAIA 3 was conceived 20 years ago to fill aviation needs for the next 25 years -- obviously, the terminal would be almost obsolete as soon as completed. The government should carefully plan the next step: a new international airport for the coming 25 years. And this time, let us do it right.

notable_anecdotes: The Piatco-vs-AEDC P17.75-billion-vs-P135-million bid disparity -- Piatco won by offering 131x more than AEDC -- 'AEDC guaranteed at least P135 million, but Piatco offered P17.75 billion!' -- the exclamation mark intact, among CJP's rare uses of typographic emphasis for shock-value.

The CJP-puzzlement framing -- 'for reasons I cannot fathom up to now' -- among the most autobiographically candid moments in CJP's column corpus, expressing two-decade-old institutional bewilderment at the government's choice of expropriation over the Puno-ponencia-prescribed police-power takeover.

The Agan v. Piatco CJP-separate-opinion quotation -- 'being riddled with irregularities galore and blatant violations of law and public policy, far too many to ignore' -- among CJP's most-quoted of his own judicial-pronouncements, fittingly self-cited in this self-vindication column.

CJP's practical-suggestion in his separate opinion -- bid out the operation under BOT-analogous principles with payment-to-builder built into the bids alongside annual guaranteed government payments -- among the rare instances of CJP-as-sitting-justice articulating a practical-administrative remedy beyond the doctrinal ruling.
The 'both the Supreme Court's ruling on temporary takeover and my practical suggestion were ignored' lament -- CJP's gentle institutional-reproach against the post-2003 executive branch.

The retired-Justice-Feliciano-consultation recommendation -- re-encountering the FLP-circle figure (last seen in C106 retiring-from-SC list and as Chamber of Mines counsel) here as Philippine counsel in the third ICSID panel.
The Fraport AG German-shareholder ICSID-second-panel initiative -- a foreign-investor-driven procedural maneuver that annulled the first panel's dismissal and reopened the compensation claim.

The 'obviously then, the terminal would be almost obsolete as soon as it is completed' diagnosis -- a single sentence capturing the absurd-arithmetic of 20-years-construction + 25-year-design-life = obsolete-on-opening reality.
The 'let us do it right' closing -- among CJP's rare unqualified-imperative closings, betraying genuine frustration with the two-decade saga.
